teaser: The sunset is magnificent. Then you notice what is in the water.
review_notes:
Zong massacre: figures vary between about 130 and 142 people thrown overboard; £30 per person was the insured value.
Link to Thomas Clarkson's history (new edition 1839) and to the 1840 anti-slavery convention in London is the standard account, not proven intent.
Ruskin's father bought the picture for him (given at New Year 1844); Ruskin sold it in 1872; MFA Boston acquired it in 1899.
Mark Twain's “tortoise-shell cat having a fit in a platter of tomatoes” appears in A Tramp Abroad (1880), quoted from a Boston newspaperman.
The small raised shapes near the floating chains (about 0.41, 0.81) are read as hands; they are tiny in this image.
Dimensions 90.8 x 122.6 cm.

lesson.text: Thirty pounds. In 1781 that was the insurance value of one enslaved African aboard the British ship Zong. Short of drinking water and far off course, the crew threw more than 130 living men, women and children into the Atlantic. Back in England, the owners filed a claim for lost cargo.

The case went to court as an insurance dispute. Nobody was tried for murder. But the story spread, and it became one of the sharpest weapons of the abolitionists, the campaigners working to end slavery. Nearly sixty years later it was back in print in London, in a new edition of a history of the slave trade. Turner seems to have read it.

In 1840 he exhibited this canvas at the Royal Academy under a long title: Slavers Throwing Overboard the Dead and Dying, Typhon Coming On. A slaver is a slave ship. A typhon is a typhoon, a violent sea storm. The name everyone uses now, The Slave Ship, came later.

What most people see first is the sky: a sun going down in a blaze of yellow, orange and blood red, split by a white shaft of light. It is one of the most gorgeous sunsets in all of painting. Turner wants you to enjoy it for a few seconds. Then he wants you to drop your eyes to the bottom right corner.
Something is sticking up out of the waves in the lower right, surrounded by fish and gulls. Find it.

spots.title: A shackled leg
spots.text: A dark human leg rises from the water, an iron ring still locked around the ankle. Fish with round staring eyes crowd in below it. This is all we see of one person.

lesson.text: The shock is designed. Turner hides the horror in the corner where a painter would normally sign, and lets beauty carry you there unprepared. Once you have seen the leg, the red in the sky stops being a sunset color. You cannot unsee it, and the foreground turns out to be full of the same story.

lesson.title: In the water
lesson.text: The brown, churning sea in the lower half is not empty. Three places tell you what the ship has just done.

spots.title: Floating chains
spots.text: Black iron shackles ride on top of a wave. Iron sinks, of course, and critics mocked Turner for it. He kept them afloat because they are the evidence.

spots.title: Hands
spots.text: Around a second set of chains, small dark shapes reach up out of the swell. They are hands. The people they belong to are still alive.

spots.title: The feeding
spots.text: Pale fish with open mouths and red, raw touches of paint. White gulls dive in from above. Nature here is not cruel, only hungry.

lesson.text: Turner hung lines of his own poetry next to the painting. They came from a long, gloomy poem called Fallacies of Hope, which he quoted for decades and never finished. The verses end by asking hope where its market is now, a bitter pun on the trade in human beings.

And the ship? It is small, off to the left, with its sails rolled up tight against the coming wind. It is leaving. Turner gives it no faces, no captain, no villain to hate. The guilty are simply sailing away, straight into a wall of dark weather that is closing in from the edge of the canvas.
Turner makes you feel the crime through your own reaction: first pleasure at the sunset, then horror, then shame at the pleasure.

Was he late to the cause? Britain had banned its slave trade in 1807 and ended slavery in most of its colonies in the 1830s. But slavery was thriving in the United States, Brazil and elsewhere, and in June 1840, weeks after the exhibition opened, campaigners from many countries met in London for a world anti-slavery convention. The picture spoke to the present.

The reviews were brutal. Critics laughed at the colors and the floating iron. Decades later the American writer Mark Twain repeated a newspaperman's joke that the painting looked like a tortoise-shell cat having a fit in a platter of tomatoes.

One reader of those reviews disagreed completely. John Ruskin, a young critic who would become the most powerful art writer in Victorian Britain, declared that if he had to stake Turner's lasting fame on a single work, it would be this one. His father bought it for him as a New Year's present.

Ruskin lived with it for 28 years. Then he sold it, saying the subject had become too painful to have in the house. It crossed the Atlantic to the United States, a country that had fought a civil war over slavery only a few years before, and in 1899 it entered the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston.

Turner never saw a typhoon, and he never crossed an ocean. His longest sea voyages were Channel crossings to the European continent. The storm here is built from decades of watching the English coast, and from memory and imagination.

spots.title: The slaver
spots.text: Thin red-brown masts tilt against the glare, sails furled. The hull is half buried in white foam. Turner paints the ship almost as lightly as the spray.

spots.title: The white shaft
spots.text: A column of pale paint cuts down through the sunset to the horizon, like a blade or a pillar of light. It divides the sky in two.

spots.title: The typhoon
spots.text: Purple-gray darkness swallows the left edge. This is the storm of the title, arriving on the side the ship is heading for.

spots.title: The great wave
spots.text: Gray-green water heaves up in thick, curling strokes. Turner dragged and scraped the paint so the sea has real ridges you could feel with a fingertip.

spots.title: A sea creature
spots.text: A large fish, more monster than animal, noses in from the right with a dark round eye. Turner's sea life is closer to nightmare than to natural history.

spots.title: Red on the water
spots.text: The sun's reflection runs down the sea in yellow and deep red. After the foreground, it is hard to read that red as light alone.

lesson.text: Stand in front of it in Boston today and the first few seconds still go the same way. The sunset pulls you in from across the room. Whether it is right for a painting about mass murder to be this beautiful is a question people have argued over ever since 1840. Turner left it open.

quiz.question: What real event lies behind the painting?
options: The crew of the Zong throwing enslaved people overboard in 1781
A naval battle against slave traders
quiz.explanation: The Zong's crew threw more than 130 people into the sea, and the owners claimed insurance.

quiz.question: What is visible in the lower right corner?
options: A shackled leg surrounded by fish and gulls
quiz.explanation: A chained leg rises from the water as fish and gulls close in.

quiz.question: Why did critics mock the chains?
options: There were too many of them
Iron chains would sink, not float
quiz.explanation: Turner kept them on the surface as evidence, even though iron sinks.

quiz.question: Who owned the painting for 28 years before selling it as too painful?
quiz.explanation: Ruskin's father bought it for him, and he later sold it.

quiz.question: Where is the ship heading in the picture?
options: Into the dark storm on the left
Toward a harbor on the right
quiz.explanation: It sails away toward the typhoon closing in from the left edge.

facts.text: Turner painted the storm after crossing the Atlantic himself.
facts.explanation: He never crossed an ocean; his sea journeys were short Channel crossings.

facts.text: The Zong case first reached court as an insurance claim, not a murder trial.
facts.explanation: The owners claimed for lost “cargo,” and nobody was tried for murder.

facts.text: The Slave Ship was the title Turner gave the painting in 1840.
facts.explanation: He called it Slavers Throwing Overboard the Dead and Dying, Typhon Coming On.
